Modelled on the low-pass effect boxes built on the synthesizer's filter.

label: Memento Delay
summary: bucket-brigade delay in the style of the late-1970s American analogue echo pedals: dark, smeared repeats with chorus and vibrato
description: A modelled bucket-brigade delay of the pedal kind, for guitars, keys, and synths: one long chain of capacitors that a clock passes the signal along, between a compressor and an expander. The delay is the line's length over the clock's rate, so the longer the delay, the slower the clock and the darker each repeat; the compander keeps the line's hiss down and lets the repeats swell and smear. Delay, feedback up to where the repeats grow by themselves, blend, the level into the line, which clips it when turned up, and the echo's level; a chorus or vibrato that swings the clock, which bends every repeat in pitch; and a standard or a long line, some 43 to 410 ms or 112 ms to 1.1 s. Modelled on the large bucket-brigade echo pedal of the late 1970s with chorus and vibrato.

label: Clementine Phaser
summary: four-stage phaser in the style of the 1970s one-knob phaser pedals: a swirling sweep
description: A modelled four-stage phaser of the one-knob pedal kind, for guitars, electric pianos, and synths: four all-pass stages, each an operational amplifier whose corner a junction field-effect transistor sets, the four gates swept together by a relaxation oscillator through the bias network, and the input summed with the fourth stage, which puts two notches in the sound that sweep up and down. The transistors' resistance goes as their gate's volts, so the sweep is not even in octaves: it passes quickly through the lows and lingers in the upper middle, and their square law adds a little even distortion on loud notes. A rate knob, as the pedal has, a depth and a mix beside it, and a switch between the earlier version and the later one, whose feedback resistor raises peaks beside the notches. Modelled on the orange phaser pedal of the mid-1970s.

label: Rotary Speaker
summary: rotating speaker in the style of the mid-century organ cabinets: the swirl, slow, fast and the sweep between
description: A modelled rotating speaker cabinet, built from its mechanism: a valve amplifier that overdrives into a crossover near 800 Hz, a horn turning above it and a drum below, slow, fast or stopped, each reaching its speed in its own time; the pitch moved by each mouth's Doppler shift, the level by where it points, and what it sends back off the cabinet's walls; two microphones, their spread and distance. For organs, guitars, electric pianos and synths. Switching speed while it plays sweeps between them.

label: Neon Tremolo
summary: opto tremolo in the style of the 1960s American amp tremolos: throb for guitar and keys
description: A modelled optical tremolo of the American amplifier kind, for guitars, electric pianos, and organs: a valve oscillator drives a neon lamp sealed with a photocell, and the cell turns the signal down as the lamp lights it. The lamp flashes once a swing, the intensity setting how brightly, and the cell darkens fast and lets go slowly, so the throb is not a sine: it falls in a few milliseconds and climbs back over tens of them. Speed and intensity, as the amplifier has, and an output. Both sides through one cell. Modelled on the tremolo of the black-panel American combos of the mid-1960s.

label: Not Out Class A
summary: class-A preamp and EQ channel in the style of the 1970s British console modules: thick, warm tracks
description: A modelled console channel of the class-A kind, for shaping single tracks: a line transformer, a stepped gain switch, an amplifier of three transistors, an equaliser of switched frequencies, and an output amplifier whose last transistor drives a gapped output transformer. A shelf at 12 kHz, a presence band at 360 Hz to 7.2 kHz on coils, a low shelf at 35, 60, 110, or 220 Hz, and a high-pass of 18 dB an octave at 50, 80, 160, or 300 Hz, with switches for the equaliser and the phase and a trim. Turned up, the output stage runs out of current and its transformer fills on low notes, so the lows thicken and distort first, mostly in the second and third harmonics. In stereo, each channel through its own circuits, with a quality switch for how far above the sample rate they are solved. Modelled on the British microphone and line amplifier with equaliser of the early 1970s, built on discrete class-A amplifier cards between transformers.

label: Punch Desk Strip
summary: discrete console channel strip in the style of the 2000s American desks: punchy preamp, proportional-Q EQ and VCA dynamics for every track
description: A modelled console channel strip of the American discrete kind, for every track of a mix: a microphone or line preamplifier with a pad, a phase switch and a low cut, a passive sweep filter (a high-pass of 12 dB an octave and a low-pass of 6), a gate or expander with a threshold, a depth, a release or hold and a fast attack, a VCA compressor with a threshold, a continuous ratio up to a limiter, three attacks, a release, a soft or hard knee and feedback or feed-forward detection that keeps the level the same as it compresses, a four-band equaliser of stepped frequencies and gains whose bands narrow as they rise, or a ten-band graphic equaliser in its place, before or after the dynamics or into their sidechain, and a fader. Modelled on the channel of the American discrete consoles of the 2000s.

label: Big Desk Strip
summary: console channel strip in the style of the 1980s British large-format desks: EQ and dynamics for every track
description: A modelled console channel strip of the later, cleaner kind, for every track of a mix: an input trim and a phase switch, a high-pass of 18 dB an octave and a low-pass of 12, a four-band equaliser whose low and high bands are shelves that switch to bells and whose two middle bands are fully parametric, with the console's two voicings of how a band's width follows its gain, a compressor with a continuous ratio up to a limiter, a threshold, an attack, a release, a fast attack switch, and automatic make-up, an expander or gate with a threshold, a range, a release, and a fast attack, switches that put the dynamics before or after the equaliser and the filters or the equaliser into the dynamics' sidechain, and an output trim. Clean operational amplifiers and voltage-controlled amplifiers: its character is its equaliser's curves and its dynamics' timing. Modelled on the channel strip of the large British mixing console of the 1980s with its four-band equaliser and channel dynamics.

label: Mastering Vari-Mu
summary: balanced variable-mu valve compressor in the style of the 1990s American mastering limiters: smooth, transparent control of whole mixes
description: A modelled variable-mu valve compressor and limiter for masters: a balanced pair of valves between an input and an output transformer, whose gain the sidechain turns down by taking both grids further under their cathodes, fed back from the output through a valve rectifier. Input, threshold, attack and output dials from 0 to 10, a recovery switch of five places from 8 s to 0.2 s, Compress or Limit, a high-pass in the sidechain, the two channels linked or apart, left and right or middle and side, and a mix. The ratio grows with the reduction, so its knee softens as it limits more. Modelled on the balanced valve limiters of the 1990s American mastering rooms.

label: Lockjaw Leveler
summary: transistor level controller in the style of the 1960s American podium limiters: aggressive, pumping, distorting; lo-fi drum and vocal crush
description: A modelled 1960s podium-microphone level controller, the cheap transistor box on a 9 V battery that locks its output once a voice passes its threshold, made over into a studio processor: crush drives it (a diode shunt turned down by a feedback detector: a fast attack, a release that holds when driven past its range, pumping), distortion drives its output stage into clipping, darkness is a low-pass from 20 kHz to 500 Hz, a slow or fast release, and a mix for parallel crushing.

label: Zener Diode Limiter
summary: diode-bridge limiter in the style of the late-1960s British studio consoles: a zener threshold, gentle compression to firm limiting, a THD rounding
description: A modelled limiter of the British studio consoles of the late 1960s, as a modern two-channel unit re-made it: a diode bridge across the audio whose conductance a feedback sidechain sets, its threshold a zener diode's. An input switch and its Low or High gain, attack and release switches (2 and the six vintage recovery times 3, 6, 10, 15, 18 and 21 among the new), the output, Comp 1 (gentle, slow), Comp 2 (its curve, faster) or Limit, a high-pass in the sidechain, THD (the bridge following the wave itself, a rounding that never clips), the two channels linked or apart, left and right or middle and side.

label: Mid-Century Vari-Mu
summary: variable-mu valve compressor in the style of the late-1950s American broadcast limiters: slow, gentle glue for masters and buses
description: A modelled variable-mu valve compressor, for masters and drum buses: a push-pull pair of remote-cutoff valves between an input and an output transformer, whose gain falls smoothly as the sidechain takes their grids further under their cathodes. The ratio is no switch's: it grows with the reduction, from a gentle slope at the knee to a limiter's well over it. An input knob in dB that drives the valves and sets the threshold with the threshold knob, a time constant switch of six places, four fixed and two automatic that let a short peak go quickly and a long passage slowly, the sidechain's bias trimmer, an output knob, a mix, a balance trimmer for the pair, a high-pass in the sidechain, a link between the two channels, a matrix that compresses their middle and side, and a sidechain from another track. The gain cell is a circuit solved part by part; the timing network is the circuit's, solved exactly. Modelled on the large American valve limiter of the late 1950s, two channels of it in one unit.

label: Blower Box
summary: valve character compressor: one-knob thickening for drums and bass
description: A valve character compressor, for thickening drums, bass, and buses with compression and valve saturation working together: one compress knob that lowers the threshold, steepens the ratio, and brings its own make-up, an attack and a release that scale a detector of two parts, a fast one for hits and a slow one that holds a long loud passage down, and a valve gain stage after it, a triode solved as a circuit, that the saturation knob drives harder without making it louder: second harmonics first, then third as it clips, with its grid drawing current on peaks. A character knob and a voice switch, fat, warm, or bright, for a tone curve after the valve; a mix of what went in for parallel compression, an output, and the automatic make-up on a switch. No one unit: it is the middle of its kind, the one-knob valve compressors and the valve saturation of mixer preamps.

label: Moonladder
summary: transistor ladder filter in the style of the late-1960s American modular filters: a warm 24 dB low-pass that sings
description: A modelled transistor ladder low-pass filter, the one in the classic American three-oscillator portable monosynth of the early 1970s, as an effect: an input pair, four transistor pairs stacked over it with a capacitor across each, an output amplifier, and the emphasis fed from the output back to the input pair. Its four poles fall 24 dB an octave; emphasis thins the bass, peaks the corner, and near the top of its travel sings by itself; drive pushes the input pair into its curve, warm and thick on the second harmonic. Cutoff from -5 to 5 as the instrument's panel has it, emphasis and drive from 0 to 10, an output, and a light quality at about half the processing.

label: Class Clean Combo
summary: clean combo in the style of the late-1960s American twin-speaker amps: big cleans that break up late
description: A modelled American clean guitar combo of two channels, without its speakers or reverb: in each channel an input valve that drives a passive treble, middle, and bass stack straight from its plate, a volume with a bright switch, and a second valve; the vibrato channel has a third after a large divider, more gain, and an optical tremolo. A long-tailed phase inverter and four beam tetrodes in fixed bias with a strong feedback loop give a big, clean power stage that breaks up late, on two speakers' load. Volume, treble, middle, and bass, bright, the channel and the high or low input, the tremolo with its speed and intensity, and a quality switch for how far above the sample rate the circuit is solved. It wants a cabinet after it, the speaker cabinet device. Modelled on the 100-watt two-speaker combo with the black panel of the mid-1960s, the clean sound of country, soul, and session guitar, built from its published drawing.

label: Icebox Bass Stack
summary: all-valve bass stack in the style of the late-1960s American 300-watt heads: the growl of rock and metal bass
description: A modelled all-valve bass head of 300 watts with its 8x10 cabinet, both its channels: in each an input valve, the ultra low switch into the volume with the ultra high switch's capacitor round it, a second valve and a passive bass and treble stack, the first with a middle of three frequencies and a bass cut; and a power stage of six output valves on a stiff supply, with no master, so the volume drives the power stage too. Volume, bass, middle, and treble, the channel, ultra high, ultra low, the normal or bright jack, and the cabinet on or off. Modelled on the 1969 rock bass head and its fridge-sized cabinet, built from its published drawing.

label: Flipside Bass Combo
summary: flip-top bass combo in the style of the 1960s American studio amps: round, soft bass
description: A modelled 1960s flip-top bass combo with its sealed 1x15: two channels, the 1964 preamp and the 1966 one, each two valve stages with a volume and a passive bass and treble, into a small push-pull pair of beam tetrodes on a valve rectifier that sags, with no master. Volume, bass, and treble, the channel, the jack, the bias of either year, and the cabinet on or off. Round and soft, the studio and soul bass sound: modelled on the flip-top combo of the 1960s.

label: Halfglow Bass Head
summary: hybrid bass head: valve preamp, solid-state punch
description: A modelled hybrid bass head with its cabinet: a valve preamp with a gain, bright, ultra high and ultra low, an active bass, a middle of five frequencies and a treble, a valve drive stage of its own, a nine-band graphic EQ, and a solid-state power amp behind a master. Punchy and tight: modelled on the rack-era hybrid bass head.

label: Delay
description: Repeats in time with the project or free: clean, tape, lo-fi, diffuse, or reversed, with filters, wobble, ping pong, and ducking, by its own input or by a sidechain.

label: Reverb
description: A space to ring in: room, hall, plate, or a shimmer whose tail climbs in pitch, with pre-delay, damping, a size to sweep, a freeze, and ducking, by its own input or by a sidechain.

label: Gemini Plate
summary: plate reverb in the style of the late-1950s German studio plates: dense, bright tails for vocals and snare
description: A plate reverberator modelled as a plate: a thin sheet of steel one metre by two, under tension, with one driver, two pickups for left and right, and a damping plate whose distance sets the decay. The sheet is some twenty-seven thousand modes of bending waves, each ringing at its own frequency and dying at its own rate, so the lows ring long and the highs short, the highs of a hit arrive before its lows, and the tail is dense from the start. Decay is the damper, from half a second to five and a half at low frequencies, and can be moved while the plate rings; pre-delay, low cut, high cut, width, mix, output, and a quality switch for a lighter plate with fewer modes. Both sides of the audio drive the one driver. Modelled on the large German studio plate reverberator of the late 1950s, the usual reverb for vocals and snare drums.

label: Concrete Echo Chamber
summary: studio echo chamber in the style of the 1950s Hollywood underground chambers: a real room's dense, dark bloom
description: A studio echo chamber modelled as a room: a bare room of shellacked concrete under the studio, a loudspeaker at one end fed from the console's echo send, and two microphones whose signals come back as the return. Each of its four rooms has its size, its walls and its speaker; the time each band rings comes from them and from the air, which takes the highs on every metre, and the first reflections are the speaker's images in the walls, heard where the microphones stand. Four pairs of microphones (valve omnis, ribbons, condenser omnis, valve cardioids), moved from the speaker to the far end; decay hangs absorbent in the room, down to about a second; pre-delay and a low cut on the send, three bands and width on the return, mix and output. Modelled on the underground chambers of a 1950s Hollywood studio.

label: Drip Spring
summary: spring reverb in the style of the early-1960s American outboard tanks: drip and boing for surf guitar and dub
description: A spring reverb tank of the kind built into guitar amplifiers and sold as studio units, modelled as its springs: two or three long coil springs, each driven at one end and heard at the other, each a bank of modes of one kind of wave whose speed falls as its pitch rises, so a hit comes out as a chirp, lows first, and comes back as a longer one each time it has been to the far end and back: the drip and the boing of surf guitar. Dwell drives the valve amplifier that drives the tank, and a loud transient overdrives it into a crash; tone is a shelf on what comes back. Decay, a short or a long tank, two or three springs panned across the sides, pre-delay, width, mix, and output. No latency.

label: 1978 Digital Hall
summary: 1970s digital hall reverb: lush, dark halls and plates for vocals and snares
description: A digital hall reverb of the late 1970s, modelled as its algorithm: a network of delays and diffusers that recirculate at a low sample rate between steep converter filters, so the tail is dark above 8 kHz and grainy far down, with its delays wandering slowly so it never rings. Nine programs: two small halls, a large hall, a chamber, a room, three plates, and a chorus. Bass and mid decay times split at a crossover, a treble decay, depth (how far back the sound sits), pre-delay, diffusion, wander and chorus for the delays' motion, the converters' hiss, mix, and output. Edits never stop the tail.

label: 1976 Digital Reverb
summary: the first digital reverb: a dense, smooth, dark tail for vocals, drums and keys
description: The first digital reverb, of the mid-1970s, modelled as its algorithm: a long loop of memory with many taps between converters of a short word with gain ranging, at a low sample rate behind steep filters, so the tail is dense, smooth, and dark above 11 kHz. A time of 0.4 to 4.5 s, with the lows and the highs at multiples of it, and pre-delay; beside the reverb, its programs of two delays, phasing, chorus, echo, and a long space. The converters' hiss, mix, and output. Edits never stop the tail.

label: 1981 Digital Ambience
summary: 1980s digital reverb: tight ambience, gated nonlinear and reverse drums
description: A digital reverb of the early 1980s, modelled as its algorithm and known for its programs: the short, dense ambience that puts a drum in a room, rooms, halls, and plates, the gated nonlinear program whose sound holds and then stops, a reverse that swells and stops, echoes, a chorus, and a freeze. A tapped early field and a recirculating loop at a clock of its own between steep converter filters. Pre-delay, decay with low and high multipliers, the converters' hiss, mix, and output. Edits never stop the tail.

label: Filter
description: A modelled analogue filter: a transistor ladder, a squelchy diode ladder, a screaming Sallen-Key, a polished OTA cascade, or a smooth state variable, driven into saturation and ringing at high resonance, as low-, band-, or high-pass, with an LFO and an envelope follower to move its cutoff. The follower listens to the filter's input or another track by sidechain.

label: Crossover
description: Splits the signal into two, three, or four bands at frequencies that are set, each band to go through a chain of devices of its own, and sums them after. With the chains empty it leaves the level as it was.

label: Mid/Side
description: Splits the signal into its middle, what the two channels share, and its sides, what they differ by, each to go through a chain of devices of its own, and puts them together after. With both chains empty it changes nothing.

label: Modular
description: A modular synth that plays the track's notes: patch sample-rate oscillators, filters, envelopes, sequencers, utilities, effects and ordinary devices with polyphonic voltage cables.

label: Effects Rack
description: Chains of devices side by side: the signal goes through each chain, and what they give is summed. Each chain has a level, a pan, a mute, and a solo, for a blend of a sound with what a chain makes of it, or of several treatments of one sound.

label: Instrument Rack
description: Several instruments played as one. Each chain holds an instrument, with MIDI devices before it and audio effects after it, and has a level, a pan, a mute, and a solo. Every chain plays every note, for layers, unless it is given a range of keys or of velocities, for a split keyboard or a sound that changes with how hard a key is struck.

label: Drum Rack
description: Pads, each for one key, each with an instrument and effects of its own: a kit built a sound at a time. A pad gives its instrument middle C, so a sample sounds as it was recorded on any pad, and pads of one choke group cut each other off, as a closed hi-hat cuts an open one: the pad's whole output fades down in 5 ms, including its effects. A mouse strike is softer at the top and harder at the bottom.
